overview: This record describes the modern Syrian state, not every ancient civilization in the Syrian region. Its atlas start in 1945 falls within a longer independence process. Five imported border intervals cover 1945 to 2020, although the index leaves the country’s lifetime open. Their outline cannot show the union with Egypt, occupation, changing fronts or recent control. Political changes did not erase Syria’s communities; the dated examples below describe particular places and institutions.

periods.title: Independence and the early republic
periods.summary: French troops left in 1946; the republic experienced repeated political upheaval.

periods.title: Union with Egypt
periods.summary: Syria belonged to the United Arab Republic before seceding in 1961.

periods.title: Restored republic and Baath ascendancy
periods.summary: The March 1963 coup brought a Baathist-led government to power.

periods.title: Assad rule before the uprising
periods.summary: Hafez al-Assad took power in 1970; his son Bashar succeeded him in 2000.

periods.title: Uprising and internationalized war
periods.summary: Protests developed into a devastating conflict involving many armed actors.

periods.title: Transition after December 2024
periods.summary: The Assad government fell on 8 December 2024; rebuilding political institutions remained a major task.

items.text: Independence came in stages. The United States recognized Syria in 1944, before the atlas begins. French troops withdrew in April 1946, and Syrians celebrated Evacuation Day on 17 April. These different milestones explain why a single founding year can be misleading.

Syria and Egypt united on 22 February 1958 as the United Arab Republic. Syria seceded on 28 September 1961. Then the 8 March 1963 coup installed a government in which Baathists held many cabinet seats. The atlas’s separate Syria outline does not display the union’s shared political institutions.

Hafez al-Assad seized power in November 1970 and remained ruler until his death in 2000, when Bashar succeeded him. This was authoritarian rule, not an uninterrupted series of freely competing governments. In February 1982, government forces devastated Hama while crushing an armed uprising; civilians suffered on a vast scale.

sections.title: War and a dated account of transition

items.text: Antigovernment protests began in March 2011, and government repression helped turn unrest into armed conflict. Opposition factions, Kurdish-led forces and Islamic State controlled different areas at different times. Russia and Iran backed Assad, while the United States supported forces fighting Islamic State and Türkiye intervened in the north. One country color cannot tell this story.

Assad’s government fell on 8 December 2024. The UN called for an inclusive political transition rather than revenge. During 2025, interim authorities established a new constitutional framework and cabinet. A change of government did not automatically restore homes, reunite families or settle all disputes over power.

On 30 January 2026, the UN Secretary-General welcomed an agreement between the Syrian government and the Syrian Democratic Forces. He called for peaceful integration of the northeast, protection of Kurdish rights and safe, voluntary returns for displaced people. An agreement is a step to implement, not proof that every local dispute has ended.

The Euphrates Dam, also called Tabqa or Thawra Dam, was completed in 1973 and created a large reservoir upstream of Raqqa. The 1988 country study describes irrigation improvements in the northeast alongside substantial cereal and cotton production. These projects changed the working landscape; their completion alone does not tell us how benefits and costs were shared.

A 1997 Syrian 200-pound note in the British Museum shows a woman at a cotton loom, workers, a cotton plant and a factory. Money placed agriculture and textile production in everyday view. The design celebrates selected kinds of work; it is not a photograph of every worker’s conditions.

UNESCO’s 2024 account of Aleppo soap-making describes olive oil and laurel oil cooked with lye. The mixture cools in a huge slab on the factory floor. Craftspeople put on large wooden shoes and use their weight with a rake to cut it into cubes. Imagine having a floor made of soap!

Each soap cube receives a hand-stamped family name. Stacked towers or pyramids let air circulate while the soap dries for six to nine months. Children learn parts of the work within craft families, including collecting olives and berries. A bar of soap can carry both a practical skill and a family signature.

In Al-Mrah near Damascus, the rose harvest begins in May. UNESCO’s 2019 record describes families picking flowers early, sorting buds for tea and preparing petals for distillation. Women make rose syrup, jam and pastries together while singing. These flowers can end up in a teacup or dessert as well as a perfume bottle.

Damascene shadow theatre makes jokes with handmade puppets behind a lit screen. Karakoz and his clever friend Eiwaz exchange comic social observations; talking animals can join them. UNESCO’s 2018 record describes a tradition once common in cafes but threatened by displacement and changing entertainment habits. Preserving it means teaching performance skills as well as keeping puppets.

sections.title: Learning, health and the practical importance of toilets

items.text: Article 28 of the 1950 constitution says: التربية والتعليم حق لكل مواطن. Read it as al-tarbiya wa-l-taʿlīm ḥaqq li-kull muwāṭin, meaning “Upbringing and education are a right of every citizen.” The Arabic here follows a later transcription of that historical text, not an original 1950 printed page. A constitutional promise does not prove that every child could attend school.

At Al Tabni school in Deir ez-Zor, damaged toilets once meant that twelve-year-old Sohaib waited until he got home, or children used nearby houses. Repairs finished in December 2022. UNICEF’s November 2023 report describes sixteen functioning classrooms and a preschool classroom. Safe bathrooms were part of making school usable again, not an optional decoration.

At Nazih Munzer School in Jaramana, 2025 repairs added solar power, safer drinking areas, ramps, handrails and an accessible toilet. UNICEF reported more than 2,300 pupils attending in two shifts. The improvements brought ordinary comforts back into lessons: desks that worked, brighter classrooms, space to play and a bathroom children could reach.

In August 2025, vaccination teams from Al-Sham Paediatric Speciality Hospital walked between tents at Al-Burj camp in Idlib. They carried coolers, announced their arrival with a loudspeaker and spoke with parents. These teams brought care directly to families at the camp. This is one documented campaign, not a measure of nationwide access.

sections.title: Discovering and caring for older histories

items.text: In 1975, Sapienza’s archaeological mission at Ebla uncovered a major cuneiform archive. Its 2025 anniversary account distinguishes more than 17,000 inventory numbers from roughly 5,000 tablets. Those ancient records transformed understanding of third-millennium BCE government and economic life. Their modern discovery belongs here; the ancient kingdom itself was a different society, thousands of years before this republic.

The ancient limestone Lion of Al-lāt from Palmyra was damaged by Islamic State in 2015. Syrian antiquities staff moved its fragments to Damascus, and a Polish restorer worked on it with UNESCO support. Restoration was completed in 2017. Between the lion’s legs sits an antelope: the monument survived through painstaking work on broken stone.

ending.text: Syria’s population and state did not disappear when Assad rule ended in December 2024. The transition remained unfinished in the UN’s 22 June 2026 briefing, which stressed political participation, justice and concerns about continuing insecurity. This card provides dated history, not a live control map or a promise that recovery is complete.
